title: 1 Samuel 13:1–7
context: 1 Samuel 13 opens the account of Saul’s reign in earnest. After his anointing (chapters 9–10), his victory over Ammon and the renewal of the kingdom at Gilgal (chapter 11), and Samuel’s warning that king and people must fear and obey the LORD (12:14–15, 24–25), the narrative turns to the Philistine threat. Saul organizes a standing force, Jonathan strikes a Philistine garrison, and the Philistines muster an overwhelming army at Michmash. Israel’s soldiers hide or flee across the Jordan, while Saul waits at Gilgal with a trembling remnant. The section sets the scene for the test of obedience in 13:8–15.

verses.text: Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel forty-two years.
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB reads, “Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel forty-two years.” Its footnote explains that the traditional Hebrew text omits “thirty” and “forty-”, and that the WEB fills the blanks from a few manuscripts of the Septuagint. Arminian readers note the textual question plainly and do not build any doctrine on the figures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the footnote at face value: the numbers come from a few Septuagint manuscripts, while the traditional Hebrew lacks them. Paul’s sermon in Acts 13:21 speaks of Saul ruling “for forty years.” Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as a standard regnal formula with a textual gap, and neither draws theological conclusions from the uncertain numbers.

verses.text: Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel, of which two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and in the Mount of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people to their own tents.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul chooses three thousand men, two thousand with himself at Michmash and Bethel and one thousand with Jonathan at Gibeah, and sends the rest home. Arminian readers note Saul’s practical leadership in forming a standing force, a step toward the kind of king the people had asked for, one who would “fight our battles” (8:20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this is the first mention of Jonathan, who will become a central figure in the following chapters. The organization of the army is sensible, but the narrative will show that Israel’s security depends on the LORD rather than on numbers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up the confrontation with the Philistines.

verses.text: Jonathan struck the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan strikes the Philistine garrison at Geba, and Saul blows the trumpet, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!” Arminian readers note Jonathan’s initiative and courage, which begins the conflict. Saul responds by rallying the people, taking up the task for which he was anointed (9:16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the call to arms follows Jonathan’s act and that Saul uses the term “Hebrews,” which in Samuel often appears on Philistine lips or for Israelites in relation to foreigners. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of open conflict with the Philistines, a struggle God had set Saul to lead.

verses.text: All Israel heard that Saul had struck the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel was considered an abomination to the Philistines. The people were gathered together after Saul to Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel hears that Saul struck the garrison, and that Israel has become “an abomination to the Philistines.” Arminian readers note that the credit goes to Saul though Jonathan did the deed, a small detail that may hint at Saul’s concern for his own standing. The people gather to Saul at Gilgal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift of credit from Jonathan to Saul without drawing strong conclusions from it, since the king was responsible for the army’s actions. Gilgal, where the kingdom was renewed (11:15), becomes the place of testing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a transition that brings Saul to Gilgal, where Samuel had told him to wait (10:8).

verses.text: The Philistines assembled themselves together to fight with Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, eastward of Beth Aven.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines gather “thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the seashore in multitude.” Arminian readers note that the description stresses Israel’s overwhelming disadvantage, testing whether Saul and the people will trust the LORD in the face of such odds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the language of sand on the seashore, used elsewhere for vast armies, and that interpreters differ on how to understand such large numbers. The point is the impossibility of victory by human strength. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting a scene in which deliverance must come from the LORD, recalling Psalm 33:16: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an army.”

verses.text: When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were distressed), then the people hid themselves in caves, in thickets, in rocks, in tombs, and in pits.
verses.arminianNotes: Seeing their danger, the people hide “in caves, in thickets, in rocks, in tombs, and in pits.” Arminian readers note the depth of fear that grips Israel. The people respond to the threat with panic rather than trust, a real human reaction that the narrative records honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Israel’s fear shows how little the people’s security rests in their new king. Having asked for a king to fight their battles (8:20), they now hide from the enemy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a portrait of a people in crisis, setting up the question of whether Saul will act in faith and obedience.

verses.text: Now some of the Hebrews had gone over the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead; but as for Saul, he was yet in Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.
verses.arminianNotes: Some Hebrews flee across the Jordan, while Saul remains at Gilgal and “all the people followed him trembling.” Arminian readers note the pressure on Saul as his army dwindles. His decision whether to wait for Samuel will be made under real fear and in a deteriorating situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the trembling of the people prepares for Saul’s test in 13:8–15, where faith must hold steady under pressure. The narrative does not excuse disobedience because of pressure, but it does show the strain Saul faced. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heightening the tension before Samuel’s arrival.
